Welcome toGravitational Focusing

Small bodies stream towards a growing planet: which strike it, and from how far out?

How would you like to begin?

Listen to the intro

About: gravitational focusing: a planet collects small bodies from a cross-section larger than its disc

About this simulation

On screen
Main view: one plane through the line of approach, 90,000 km across and 70,000 km up at equal scale, with the planet at its true radius Rpl, a dashed centre line, the next body waiting on the left edge where its path starts, below a dotted line at height b that marks its aim (gravity has already pulled it down a little, a slow body by thousands of km), and the exact paths of fired bodies (pale blue = struck the surface, grey = missed and left). After a stream, the grazing path, its incoming asymptote and bmax are marked. Inset: the face-on view along the line of approach, −30,000 to +30,000 km, with each fired body placed at distance b from the centre.
Controls
Approach speed v∞ (3 to 12 km/s), planet mass (0.1 to 1.0 Earth masses at the Earth's mean density) and the impact parameter b of the next body (0 to 30,000 km). Fire one sends a body at b; Fire stream sends 61 bodies, b = 0 to 30,000 km in 500 km steps. Changing any control clears the trails. The Readouts panel in the sidebar shows bmax and the focusing factor once a stream has struck.
Measured
Rpl = 6371 km × M1/3; vesc from the surface; bmax is the impact parameter of the path that just grazes the surface, and σ/πRpl2 = (bmax/Rpl)2. Every path is the exact two-body hyperbola.
Assumptions
Two bodies only: the Sun's tide, the other planetesimals and gas drag are left out, so each path is an exact hyperbola and no body can be captured into an orbit. Each small body is a point that stops where it first touches the surface. v∞ is its speed relative to the planet while still far away; in a disc it is set by the random speeds of the planetesimal swarm. The planet has the Earth's mean density at every mass, so Rpl ∝ M1/3 and vesc ∝ M1/3.

Guided Inquiry

1 · One body aimed above

Set the planet mass to 1.0 Earth mass, the approach speed v∞ to 6 km/s and the impact parameter b to 8,000 km, which is larger than the planet's radius of 6,370 km. Before firing one body, predict what it does.

2 · How far the planet reaches

Keep the planet mass at 1.0 Earth mass and the approach speed at 6 km/s. Before firing a stream, predict the largest impact parameter bmax at which a body still strikes the planet.

3 · Slower bodies

Keep the planet mass at 1.0 Earth mass and lower the approach speed v∞ to 3 km/s. Before firing a stream, predict bmax.

4 · Faster bodies

Keep the planet mass at 1.0 Earth mass and raise the approach speed v∞ to 12 km/s. Before firing a stream, predict bmax.

5 · Just beyond capture

Keep the planet mass at 1.0 Earth mass, set the approach speed v∞ to 3 km/s and set b to 26,000 km, just outside the bmax of 24,600 km found in question 3. Before firing one body, predict its path.

6 · A ten times heavier planet

Set the approach speed v∞ to 4 km/s. You will fire a stream at a planet of 0.1 Earth masses and then another at a planet of 1.0 Earth mass, which has ten times the mass. Before firing either, predict how the capture cross-section σ = πbmax2 of the heavier planet compares with that of the lighter one.

7 · What you found

A planet sweeps up small bodies over a cross-section larger than its disc: σ = πRpl2(1 + vesc2/v∞2). The focusing is strong when the bodies arrive slowly, v∞ ≪ vesc.

Because vesc grows with the planet's mass, a bigger planet's σ grows faster than its mass, so it grows faster in proportion: runaway growth. This lasts only while the swarm's random speeds v∞ stay low, and the Sun's pull, left out here, also limits it.

01

At a glance

This sim fires small bodies at a planet along their exact two-body paths and shows which ones strike its surface, for each aim b, approach speed v∞ and planet mass.

What you'll learn

  • How a body's aim b and speed v∞ shape its path past a planet.
  • What sets the largest aim, bmax, that still strikes the surface.
  • How mass and speed set the capture cross-section σ, and why planets grow by runaway (notes, section 2.3).
The set-up at the opening values: a planet of radius Rpl and the next body, aimed at height b above the centre line.

What's on screen

  • Brown disc: the planet at its true radius Rpl, on the dashed centre line. White dot: the next body, at the left edge where its path starts. Dotted line: its aim, at height b; the planet has already pulled the body a little below it, a slow one by thousands of km.
  • Pale-blue trail: a body that struck the surface. Grey trail: a body that missed and left.
  • Amber path and arrows: after a stream, the grazing path and bmax.
  • Inset and Readouts: the inset shows each body at distance b, face-on.
See itLook at the opening values. Watch for: the planet, and at the left edge the next body waiting just below its dotted aim line at height b, with nothing fired yet.

03

Aimed above the surface, a body can still strike it

The impact parameter b is how far the body would miss the planet's centre if it kept to a straight line. Gravity bends the path towards the planet, so a body can strike the surface even when b is larger than Rpl (notes, section 2.3).

Per kilogram, two things stay fixed along the whole path: the angular momentum bv∞, and the energy ½v∞². The path is an exact hyperbola, and b is measured on its incoming straight line, before any bending.

The opening values: aimed at b = 8,000 km (dotted line), the body bends down and ends on the surface of the planet, Rpl = 6,370 km.

Here b is 1,630 km above the surface. Followed as a point-mass path, the body would pass within 2,590 km of the centre, which is inside the planet, so it reaches the surface first.

Key idea. A body strikes when its bent path comes within Rpl of the centre, not when its straight-line aim does.
See itFire one body at the opening values. Watch for: its trail bending down from the 8,000 km aim and ending on the planet, though it started above it.
04

The grazing path marks the largest aim that still strikes

Every path with b below bmax strikes the planet, and every path above it misses. bmax belongs to the grazing path, which touches the surface at speed vmax, at right angles to the radius. Angular momentum then gives (notes, 2.40):

Equation (2.40). b is measured from the incoming asymptote.

Energy gives vmax² = v∞² + vesc², where vesc is the escape speed from the surface. So (2.41):

Equation (2.41). Every path with a smaller b strikes.
v∞ = 6 km/s, one Earth mass: b = 10,000 km strikes, the grazing path touches, b = 17,000 km misses.

For an Earth-mass planet, vesc = 11.19 km/s. At v∞ = 6 km/s, bmax = 13,480 km, which is 2.12 Rpl. At 3 km/s it is 24,600 km, and at 12 km/s it is 8,710 km.

See itFire a stream at the opening values. Watch for: an amber grazing path and a bmax arrow appearing once the bodies land, with Grazing bmax reading 13480 km.
See itNow halve the approach speed to 3 km/s and fire another stream. Watch for: after a few seconds, the amber grazing path swinging out, with Grazing bmax reading 24600 km.
05

The capture cross-section is the disc area times a focusing factor

The planet collects every body with b below bmax. Seen face-on, that is a disc of radius bmax, so the effective cross-section is σ = πbmax². Written with vesc (2.42):

Equation (2.42). The bracket is gravitational focusing; the sim shows it as σ/πRpl² = (bmax/Rpl)².
Face-on view of a stream at the opening values. Pale blue struck, grey missed. The factor is 4.48.
v∞ Mpl b

These sliders move the sim too. The numbers come from the sim's own audit function.

When v∞ is much larger than vesc the factor is close to 1 and the cross-section is close to the disc. When v∞ is much smaller the factor is large.

See itRaise the approach speed to 12 km/s and fire a stream. Watch for: Focusing σ/πRpl² reading 1.87, and the pale-blue dots reaching only a little beyond the planet in the face-on view.
06

A close pass is not capture: the path stays a hyperbola

A body arriving from far away carries energy ½v∞² per kilogram. Gravity gives back on the way out exactly what it took on the way in, so with only two bodies the path is always a hyperbola: the body either strikes or leaves.

Just outside bmax the pass is close and the bending is large. At v∞ = 3 km/s the opening mass has bmax = 24,600 km. Aimed at b = 26,000 km, the body gets within 7,070 km of the centre, about 700 km above the surface, and its path turns through about 119° before it leaves.

Key idea. Missing the surface by a little does not mean being caught. Capture into an orbit would need something the sim leaves out: another body, the Sun's tide or gas drag.
See itSet b to 26,000 km at 3 km/s and fire one body. Watch for: a grey trail swinging round the planet just above the surface and leaving down and to the left.
07

A heavier planet collects faster than its mass alone suggests

At a fixed density, Rpl grows as Mpl1/3, so the disc area πRpl² grows only as Mpl2/3. But vesc grows as Mpl1/3 too, so the focusing factor rises with the mass.

At v∞ = 4 km/s, raising Mpl from 0.1 to 1.0 M⊕ takes vesc from 5.19 to 11.19 km/s and the factor from 2.68 to 8.82. The disc area grows 4.6 times, but σ grows about 15 times, from π(4,850 km)² to π(18,920 km)².

When v∞ is much smaller than vesc, the notes find (2.44):

Equation (2.44), with ρsol the mass density of the small bodies. It goes as Mpl4/3.

So a body that is already larger than its neighbours grows faster in proportion to its mass. The notes call this runaway growth. The sim shows only the two-body step, one planet's σ, not the swarm or the Sun's tide.

See itSet Mpl to 0.1 M⊕ and v∞ to 4 km/s, then fire a stream. Watch for: once the bodies land, Grazing bmax reading 4850 km and Focusing σ/πRpl² reading 2.68.
See itNow raise Mpl to 1.0 M⊕ and fire another stream. Watch for: Grazing bmax growing to 18920 km and Focusing σ/πRpl² reading 8.82.
08

Summary

In one line. Whether a body strikes a planet depends on its aim b, its approach speed v∞ and the planet's mass, through the grazing path that sets bmax and the cross-section σ = πbmax².
  • A body strikes when b < bmax = Rpl(1 + vesc²/v∞²)1/2.
  • σ = πRpl²(1 + vesc²/v∞²): the factor is large when v∞ is much smaller than vesc, and near 1 when it is much larger.
  • Close passes bend a path a lot, but with two bodies they never capture.

Common mix-ups

  • "Aimed above the surface means a miss." At 6 km/s, bmax = 13,480 km, so b = 8,000 km is well inside.
  • "A close flyby is captured." At 3 km/s, a 26,000 km path turns through 119° and leaves.
  • "σ grows only with the disc, as Mpl2/3." The factor grows too: at 4 km/s, σ rises about 15 times for 10 times the mass.

Things to try on your own

  • Set Mpl = 0.5 M⊕ and v∞ = 4 km/s, fire a stream, and check that Grazing bmax reads 12310 km.
